title: OpenAI Foundation Pledges $100 Million to Double Hepatitis C Cure Rates Across Eight States
excerpt: The Breakthroughs to Follow-Through initiative will use AI tools to reconnect diagnosed patients with treatment in a disease that is 95% curable but widely undertreated.
body:
• The OpenAI Foundation is investing $100 million in a new initiative with the Common Health Coalition to double hepatitis C cure rates in eight U.S. states within two years
  • The Breakthroughs to Follow-Through initiative will start in Alabama, Illinois, Louisiana, and Massachusetts, using AI to reconnect patients with treatment
  • Despite 95% cure rates with modern antiviral drugs, only one in three diagnosed Americans receives treatment within a year
  • The program may later expand to cover HIV prevention and curable cancers

The OpenAI Foundation announced a $100 million partnership with the Common Health Coalition to tackle one of American healthcare's most persistent paradoxes: a disease that is almost always curable but still affects 1.7 million people because most diagnosed patients never receive treatment.

The initiative, called Breakthroughs to Follow-Through, will deploy AI-powered tools to help states and local health departments identify hepatitis C patients who have fallen out of care, reconnect them with treatment, and reduce the administrative burden on healthcare workers, the coalition announced on August 13.

The Treatment Gap

Direct-acting antiviral drugs cure more than 95% of hepatitis C patients who complete an 8-to-12-week course, typically with minimal side effects. Yet only about one in three Americans diagnosed with the infection actually receives treatment within a year. The gap between medical breakthrough and patient access has persisted for years despite the availability of effective therapies.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=yPM-FdjBGrc

The initiative aims to at least double cure rates in its target states and localities within two years. The rollout begins in Alabama, Illinois, Louisiana, and Massachusetts, with additional states expected to join within six months. Eight states total will participate in the initial phase.

"Hospitals and health systems are committed to ensuring more people have access to curative hepatitis C treatment, and innovative AI tools can help care teams identify eligible patients, connect them to treatment and ultimately improve the health of communities nationwide."

— Michelle Hood, AHA Executive Vice President and COO

AI as Infrastructure, Not Cure

The program's approach is notably practical. Rather than using AI to discover new drugs or treatments, it targets the logistics of care delivery — finding patients who were diagnosed but never treated, streamlining care coordination, and cutting paperwork that slows treatment access.

Anna Makanju, who leads AI for Civil Society and Philanthropy at the OpenAI Foundation, framed the project as a model for how AI can support public health at the community level. Organizations closest to these challenges often understand community needs best but lack the technical resources to deploy AI tools effectively, she said.

The American Hospital Association is a founding partner of the Common Health Coalition, which also includes AHIP, the Alliance of Community Health Plans, the American Medical Association, and Kaiser Permanente. ChangeLab Solutions serves as the coalition's host organization.

Part of a Larger Push

The hepatitis C initiative sits within the OpenAI Foundation's broader commitment to disease research. Earlier this year, the foundation finalized more than $100 million in grants across six research institutions for Alzheimer's research. It has announced plans to invest at least $1 billion in 2026 across life sciences, economic impact, AI resilience, and community programs, as part of a $25 billion long-term commitment to curing diseases and AI resilience.

The $100 million for hepatitis C is distinct from those research grants. Where the Alzheimer's funding supports scientific discovery, the B2F initiative addresses a problem downstream: getting proven treatments to the patients who need them.

What's Next

If the hepatitis C phase succeeds, the initiative plans to expand into HIV prevention and curable cancers. The program also coincides with a separate $100 million HHS pilot, the Hepatitis C Elimination Initiative administered by SAMHSA, which targets testing and treatment among people with substance use disorders and serious mental illness.

Together, the public and private efforts represent a significant escalation in the push to eliminate hepatitis C in the United States, shifting the challenge from one of medical science — where the problem is largely solved — to one of health system execution.
